clinicalPearls: An X-linked recessive bleeding disorder affecting mainly males; haemophilia A results from factor VIII deficiency and haemophilia B from factor IX deficiency.
The two types are clinically indistinguishable and are separated by specific factor assays.
Disease severity correlates with residual factor activity: severe disease often presents with spontaneous bleeding, while milder forms bleed mainly after trauma or surgery.
Hallmark manifestations are deep bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis) and muscles rather than mucocutaneous bleeding.
Screening typically shows a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) with a normal prothrombin time and platelet count.
Recurrent joint bleeds lead to chronic synovitis and progressive haemophilic arthropathy if not prevented.
Management centres on replacing the deficient clotting factor, with prophylactic regimens preventing bleeds in severe disease and on-demand treatment for acute bleeds.
Development of inhibitory antibodies against the replaced factor is a major complication that reduces treatment efficacy.
Intracranial haemorrhage is a life-threatening event that warrants immediate factor replacement, and newer therapies such as non-factor agents and gene therapy are changing management.
reference.pathophysiology: Deficiency of factor VIII or factor IX impairs the intrinsic pathway of the coagulation cascade, reducing generation of activated factor X and thereby the thrombin burst required for a stable fibrin clot. Primary haemostasis (platelet plug formation) is intact, so initial bleeding may stop, but the fibrin clot is inadequate and delayed or recurrent bleeding follows, characteristically into joints and muscles. Repeated haemarthroses cause iron deposition, synovial hypertrophy, and cartilage destruction leading to chronic arthropathy.
additionalDifferentials: Other clotting factor deficiencies (e.g. factor XI)
Vitamin K deficiency or liver disease
Non-accidental injury when bruising pattern is unexplained
additionalInvestigations: aPTT, prothrombin time, and platelet count as initial screen
Specific factor VIII and factor IX activity assays
Mixing study to demonstrate factor deficiency versus inhibitor
Inhibitor (Bethesda) assay when replacement therapy is failing
Von Willebrand factor studies to exclude von Willebrand disease
Genetic testing for carrier detection and prenatal diagnosis
redFlags: Suspected intracranial haemorrhage (headache, vomiting, altered consciousness, focal signs)
Bleeding into the neck, throat, or retroperitoneum threatening the airway or causing large occult loss
Poor response to factor replacement suggesting an inhibitor
Significant bleeding after trauma or before surgery without prophylaxis
reference.prognosis: With modern factor replacement and prophylaxis, life expectancy and quality of life approach normal; outcomes worsen with inhibitor development, chronic arthropathy, and delayed treatment of major bleeds.
pitfalls: Delaying factor replacement while awaiting imaging in suspected serious bleeding
Attributing bleeding solely to trauma and missing an underlying disorder
Using aspirin or NSAIDs and intramuscular injections that increase bleeding risk
Overlooking inhibitor development when a previously effective factor dose stops working
